title: Route packing mathematical overview
sections: A finite directed graph has one Start s and a different Finish t. Every arrow has capacity one. Routes are simple directed s-to-t paths; different routes may share dots but not arrows. A closure removes an arrow, not a dot.

The greatest number of edge-disjoint routes equals the fewest arrows whose removal blocks every route (the unit-capacity max-flow/min-cut theorem). Equivalently, minimize the number of arrows leaving a set S containing s but not t. Incoming arrows do not count. A route may cross a cut more than once.

A collection of k routes and a blocking set of k arrows certify both optima. Being unable to add an unused forward route does not certify optimality. A simple residual change-walk uses unused arrows forward and reserved arrows backward; a backward step cancels a reservation. An s-to-t change-walk increases the route count by one after any cycles are removed. If none exists, the reachable dots determine a matching cut.

K-1 constructs small route collections, finds matching closures and investigates a game. Grades 2-3 organizes all small closures and encounters internal bottlenecks and rerouting. Grades 4-5 distinguishes outgoing from incoming cut arrows, cancels several reservations and can justify the general theorem.

First try routes and closures; then conjecture a maximum; finally give both sides of a certificate. The guide keeps the longer conservation and decomposition proof after the keyed problems. The theorem here is for one common endpoint pair and edge capacity, not several prescribed pairs or vertex-disjoint routes. Keep the theorem map with adults until children have explored.
